content: The term dandelion refers to species within the genus Taraxacum, a large group of flowering plants belonging to the family Asteraceae. In the Asteraceae family, what appears to be a single flower is actually a composite flower head made up of numerous small flowers called florets. Dandelions are native to Europe and Asia but have spread to many other regions. In areas where they are not native, particularly in northern regions, they have become invasive weeds, thriving in disturbed soils and human-altered environments. Species of Taraxacum reproduce asexually through a process called apomixis, allowing seed production without pollination. Dandelions are herbaceous plants with a taproot system, and they can be biennial or perennial. They are native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere in the Old World. Commonly regarded as weeds or ruderal plants, the genus is taxonomically complex, with many macrospecies and frequent polyploidy. Over 250 species have been documented in the British Isles alone, though some botanists recognize only about 60 species. The leaves of dandelions are simple, basal, and range from 5 to 25 cm in length. They can be entire or lobed and form a rosette above the central taproot. As the leaves grow outward, they suppress surrounding vegetation, such as grass, by blocking sunlight. The plant produces a bright yellow flower head, which opens during the day and closes at night, on a hollow stem (scape) that exudes a milky latex when broken. Each rosette can produce multiple flowering stems, and the flower head, measuring 2–5 cm in diameter, consists entirely of ray florets. Dandelions serve as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species. Dandelions have become established as weeds in the Americas, Australia, and New Zealand, and they are now common in temperate regions worldwide. The mature flower develops into a globe of fine filaments, which facilitate wind dispersal of the seed-containing achenes. This structure is commonly referred to as the clock. The flower head is surrounded by bracts, often mistaken for sepals, arranged in two series. The inner bracts remain erect until the seeds mature, after which they flex downward to allow seed dispersal. The outer bracts are always reflexed downward. Some species shed the parachute (pappus) from the achenes. Between the pappus and the achene is a stalk called a beak, which elongates as the fruit matures and detaches easily from the achene. The name dandelion is derived from the French term dent-de-lion, meaning lion's tooth, a reference to the sharply lobed leaves of the plant. The English spelling reflects the French pronunciation at the time the word was adopted into English. The earliest written usage of the term dates back to a 1373 herbal, though it appeared as a proper name in a 1363 document. In Norwegian, the plant is called Løvetann, also meaning lion's tooth, and similar names exist in German (Löwenzahn), Italian (dente di leone), Spanish (diente de león), and Portuguese (dente-de-leão). In Turkish, it is known as karahindiba, meaning black endive. Hungarian names include kutyatej (dog milk, referring to the white sap) and gyermekláncfű. Selected species of dandelions include Taraxacum officinale (common dandelion), Taraxacum albidum (a white-flowering Japanese dandelion), and Taraxacum japonicum (Japanese dandelion). The red-seeded dandelion (Taraxacum laevigatum) has reddish-brown achenes and deeply cut leaves, with hooded tips on the inner bracts. The genus Taraxacum is taxonomically complex due to the prevalence of triploid individuals, which reproduce asexually through apomixis. This allows seed production without fertilization, rendering flowers vestigial in function. However, some triploid dandelions produce a small percentage of fertile pollen, maintaining limited genetic exchange with sexually reproducing individuals. Diploid dandelions, on the other hand, require cross-pollination and are self-incompatible. In southern Europe and Asia, dandelion populations are sexual or mixed sexual-apomictic, while in northern regions and non-native zones, only triploid and tetraploid apomicts are found. This distribution may be influenced by factors such as temperature, pre-glacial population survival, and human activity. A single dandelion plant can produce over 2,000 seeds annually, and dense stands may yield more than 97 million seeds per hectare each year. After pollination, the dandelion flower dries out over approximately 10 days, during which the seed-bearing parachutes expand and lift out of the dried flower head. The dried flower parts fall off, and the parachute ball opens into a full sphere. When the seed strikes an obstacle, the parachute detaches, often leading to germination at the base of the obstacle. Once the seed is released, the parachutes lose their feathery structure and take on a fuzzy, cotton-like appearance, often referred to as dandelion snow. Despite being considered a weed by many gardeners, dandelions have culinary and medicinal uses. They are cultivated on a small scale as a leaf vegetable and can be consumed cooked or raw in soups and salads. The young leaves and unopened buds are typically eaten raw, while older leaves are cooked. Raw leaves have a slightly bitter taste and are rich in vitamin A, vitamin C, and iron, containing more iron and calcium than spinach. Dandelion flowers are used to make dandelion wine, often with citrus fruits, and dandelion flower jam. Roasted dandelion root can serve as a coffee substitute and is believed to stimulate digestion when consumed before meals. Dandelion root is sold as a diuretic in Canada and is considered a liver-cleansing tonic. The plant's milky latex has been used as a mosquito repellent and for treating warts. Additionally, a dye can be extracted from the roots. The roasted roots are also marketed as a coffee-like product called Dandy Blend. In the UK, a soft drink called Dandelion and Burdock has been popular, though it is unclear if supermarket versions contain either plant. Agriculturally, dandelions are beneficial for breaking up hardpan soil with their deep roots. Dandelions contain luteolin, an antioxidant with demonstrated antioxidant properties and no cytotoxicity. They also produce caffeic acid, a secondary plant metabolite unrelated to caffeine. While some studies suggest that caffeic acid may be carcinogenic in mice, more recent research indicates that gut bacteria in rats may alter its metabolites. No adverse effects of caffeic acid have been reported in humans. Dandelions are often confused with catsears (Hypochaeris), also known as false dandelions. While both plants have similar flowers and windborne seeds, catsear stems are forked and solid, whereas dandelion stems are unforked and hollow. Both plants have a rosette of leaves and a central taproot, but dandelion leaves are jagged, while catsear leaves are lobed and hairy. Other similar plants include hawkweeds (Hieracium) and hawksbeards (Crepis), which can be distinguished by their branched flowering stems.
